entries.title: gcc
entries.description: Stages: preprocessing → compilation → assembly → linking. By default gcc does all of them.

details.name: -c
details.text: compile to an object file (`a.c` → `a.o`), do not link

details.name: -Wall -Wextra
details.text: enable the useful warnings; fix them

details.name: -L dir  -l name
details.text: directory to search for libraries; link against `libname`

entries.example:
gcc -Wall -Wextra -g main.c util.c -o prog
gcc -c util.c -o util.o
gcc main.o util.o -o prog
mistakes: Ignoring warnings: most of them are real bugs.

entries.title: Static and dynamic libraries
entries.summary: How to build and use .a and .so libraries.
entries.syntax:
ar rcs libname.a a.o b.o
gcc -shared -fPIC -o libname.so a.c b.c
gcc main.c -L. -lname -o prog
entries.description: A static library (`libname.a`, an archive of object files) is copied into the executable at link time (only the needed parts). A dynamic library (`libname.so`) is not copied: the loader finds it when the program starts, so it must be on its search path. `-lname` refers to `libname.a`/`libname.so` (the `lib` prefix and extension are implied). With dependent libraries, list the one that uses another BEFORE it.

details.name: LD_LIBRARY_PATH
details.text: environment variable with extra directories where the loader looks for `.so` files

details.name: ldd prog
details.text: lists the dynamic libraries a program needs

entries.example:
ar rcs libutil.a a.o b.o
gcc main.c -L. -lutil -o prog              # static
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./prog                       # when libutil is a .so
mistakes: Running a program linked against a `.so` that the loader cannot find.

entries.title: Modules: headers and sources
entries.summary: Splitting a program into .h and .c files.
entries.syntax:
util.h: types + prototypes (with include guard)
util.c: #include "util.h" + implementation
entries.description: The header is the interface: type definitions and function prototypes, protected against double inclusion. The source file implements it and includes its own header so the compiler checks that both agree. Functions and globals that are internal to the module are `static`. Each `.c` is compiled separately into a `.o` and the linker joins them.
mistakes: Defining (not just declaring) variables or functions in a header included from several files.

entries.title: make and Makefiles
entries.description: `make target` runs the recipe of a rule when the target does not exist or any dependency is newer. Recipe lines MUST start with a TAB. Variables (`CC=gcc`, `CFLAGS=-Wall -g`) are used as `$(CC)`. A pattern rule such as `%.o: %.c` explains how to build any object file from its source; inside a recipe `$<` is the first dependency and `$@` the target. A target that is not a file (like `clean`) is declared with `.PHONY`.
entries.example:
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -g

prog: main.o util.o
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $^ -o $@

%.o: %.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -c $< -o $@

.PHONY: clean
clean:
	rm -f *.o prog
mistakes: Using spaces instead of a TAB in recipe lines.
Forgetting `-c` in a rule that builds an object file.
